title: A Delhi Hotel Had No Fire Exit and Too Many Rooms. Twenty-One People Died Inside.
excerpt: The Flourish Stay B&B in Malviya Nagar was approved for six rooms but operated more than twenty. Most of the dead were foreign nationals who came to India for medical treatment.
body:
A fire at a bed-and-breakfast in south Delhi's Malviya Nagar killed twenty-one people on Wednesday morning, making it the capital's deadliest blaze since 2022 and exposing deep failures in a fire-safety regime that is supposed to protect millions of people who pass through the city's unregulated guesthouses every year.

The Flourish Stay B&B erupted in flames at approximately 8:48 AM. At least fifty-eight people were rescued and rushed to nearby hospitals, where twenty-one were declared dead. Eight others remain on ventilator support in critical condition, according to Dr Sandeep Budhiraja, medical director at Max Healthcare Group. Most victims suffered smoke inhalation rather than burns. Several sustained fractures after jumping from upper floors to escape.

## A Hotel Built for Six Rooms That Operated Twenty

The building had approval for six guest rooms. Investigators found more than twenty in operation, crammed into a five-storey structure in a narrow lane with a single entry and exit point. The hotel had no fire no-objection certificate. Local media reported that it was popular among patients being treated at a nearby hospital and their relatives, many of whom had travelled from overseas.

Of the twenty-one dead, seventeen were foreign nationals. Officials confirmed victims from Bangladesh, Nigeria, Mozambique, Liberia, Kenya, Cameroon, and Turkmenistan. India's Ministry of External Affairs said it is coordinating with the embassies concerned. Foreign Minister S. Jaishankar posted on X that the government was extending "all necessary assistance."

## Owner Arrested, Court Grants Police Custody

Hotel co-owner Lavkesh Bajaj was arrested hours after the fire. Delhi Police had issued a lookout circular against Bajaj and his wife immediately after the blaze. On Thursday, a magistrate at Saket Courts remanded Bajaj to four days of police custody.

The FIR against him cites Sections 105 and 326 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita — culpable homicide not amounting to murder and mischief by fire. Investigators are examining his ownership structure. Sources told reporters that Bajaj operates multiple hospitality units and is the sole owner of the building.

## A Neighbourhood in Shock

On Thursday morning, the lane around the gutted hotel fell silent. Guest houses, homestays, and shops in the surrounding area shuttered and locked their gates. Locals described occupants packing their belongings and vacating as owners shut down operations preemptively.

Residents recalled seeing people trapped inside the building, banging on glass windows and screaming for help as smoke poured through the corridors. One local told PTI that he received a call from his tenant early in the morning and initially thought his own house was on fire.

## Delhi Announces City-Wide Crackdown

The Delhi chief minister's office announced a city-wide enforcement operation against all guest houses and establishments operating in violation of fire safety norms and building bylaws. Non-compliant premises will be sealed and operators prosecuted, the government said in a post on X late Wednesday.

The crackdown faces a structural challenge. Delhi has thousands of informal guesthouses, paying guest accommodations, and unlicensed bed-and-breakfasts operating in residential areas, many without fire safety certificates. Enforcement has historically been reactive — triggered by tragedy, then tapering off as political attention moves elsewhere.

## The Diaspora Dimension

The fire has drawn attention to a little-discussed pattern in India's medical tourism infrastructure: budget accommodations clustered around major hospitals that serve foreign patients who cannot afford the medical facility's own lodging. Many of the victims at Flourish Stay had come for treatment at a nearby hospital, a pipeline that operates with virtually no regulatory oversight of the housing that sustains it.

India's medical tourism sector brings in an estimated 2 million foreign patients annually, many from South Asia and Africa. The accommodations they rely on sit in a regulatory grey zone — too small to trigger hotel licensing requirements in many jurisdictions, too transient for residential building codes to apply.

The Malviya Nagar fire is likely to prompt calls for tighter regulation of this sector. Whether those calls lead to lasting change, or follow the pattern of earlier tragedies, remains an open question. The last fire of comparable scale in Delhi killed twenty-seven people at a commercial building in Mundka in 2022. The reforms promised after that disaster remain largely unimplemented.
